matters, but I am sorry that one occupying his high and responsible position did not pay a little more attention to the facts before making the statements he uttered regarding the Esquimalt drydock. The writer in MacLean's, too, filled with enthusiasm, has departed from the high plane of journalism and attempted to be sensational in the hope of attracting attention. His statement regarding the Esquimalt drydock is very inaccurate indeed, and while it makes very excellent reading it suffers from one severe handicap

it is untrue. But if the story had been told plainly it would have lacked political sting, and no doubt this would have very seriously interfered with its commercial value. Had he taken the trouble, he could have found the facts within the pages of Hansard. Ananias and Baron Munchausen have probably gained a very much wider reputation for the extravagant and the marvellous in fiction than our friend of MacLean's; certainly they are notorious. We all know that Ananias' effort was rather disastrous to him. The Baron, I think, simply indulged in fantastic tales as a pastime, but not as a means of livelihood. Unfortunately such articles as have appeared in MacLean's recently in connection with the public service inflict severe injury on a great many people who have' no possible opportunity of defending themselves. I am now referring particularly to those who occupy positions in the Civil Service of this country, men and women who have devoted their whole lives to the public service, who have done splendid work in their time and who have played a very important part in building up Canada. Such sensational articles convey an impression throughout the land which is very unfair to those people.
I have talked often about the Esquimalt drydock and I do nci want to repeat my remarks unduly, but under the circumstances I think it is only fair to the late government, to the member for the constituency in which this drydock is situated, and to myself, that the facts should be fairly placed before the House. In the first place; no drydock is being built at Victoria, B.C., as stated by MacLean's magazine. The drydock is not in my constituency, but in that of the member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie). Then again, it is not 450 feet in length, but 430 feet, and the difference is a very important item if you are tryng to dock a ship which is a little longer than 430 feet. That drydock has been built for about forty years; it has rendered very excellent service, but it is too small for the mercantile and naval vessels that are being built to-day. During the war a number [Mr. Tolmie.,
of warships, four during one year, had to seek dock facilities in the United States owing to the small capacity of the dockage on the Pacific coast of Canada. Ali that work was lost to our Canadian workmen at a time when they needed it very badly, and the American workmen benefited accordingly. It has long been recognized that larger drydock facilities are necessary there. A site was purchased at Esquimau m either 1913 or 1914, at a place called Langs Cove. This was at least three years before I entered public life, so that the statement made in MacLean's magazine and the inference thrown out by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in the course of his remarks the other day, that the Esquimalt drydock was built for the purpose of electing Dr. Tolmie on the occasion of the by-election in 1919, are hardly correct. I was not connected with the project in any way, directly or indirectly, at the time the site v'as purchased, and I have not since then been connected with it in any way except as representative of the city of Victoria. >
Yarrows Limited, the greai Glasgow shipbuilding firm, decided to locate a branch plant somewhere on the Pacific coast, and after making a very careful survey of th4 whole of that area, both on the American side and on the Canadian side, they decided that Esquimalt was the best place to put' their plant. During the war no efforts were made to carry on construction of this dock, as might reasonably have been expected; we had other more important things to take care of. But at the conclusion cf the war strong pressure was brought to bear in the matter and every effort was made to have the work carried on to a conclusion The Hon. Mr. Car-vell, then Minister of Public Works, announced on June 27th, 1919, that the dock would be constructed. Shortly after that, very early in July, boring operations were commenced at Lang's Cove under the supervision of the Department of Public Works, with a view to the securing of such information as would be necessary in preparing the specifications. Early m July $500,000 were voted for the purpose of commencing the work. At that particular time I hid no intimation whatever that I would be offered the position of Minister of Agriculture. Some time after that, upon my return to the coast, I was offered the position, and I accepted it, and remained in the office for a period of "two years. I want to say right here that so far as the drydock is concerned my acceptance or otherwise of the position would have made

The Address-Mr. Tolmie
no difference whatever, because we felt that the drydock was a necessity and we certainly should have continued to press for its immediate construction, particularly in view of Mr. Carvell's statement that the work would proceed.
A very important ship repairing business has already been established at Esquimalt. The commerce on the Pacific has increased by leaps and bounds. The traffic over to Australia and to Asiatic ports has increased very largely during the last ten or fifteen years. Apparently this fact has not been appreciated by those who are criticising the construction of this dock. Numbers of vessels are now traversing the Pacific of a burthen of 20,000 tons, and large vessels are becoming more numerous in proportion to the small ones, so that a small drydock is of no use for their accommodation. The development of the wheat business through the port of Vancouver has been tremendous. Just the other day when I left Vancouver on my way to the opening of the House there were no less than forty-four vessels lying in the stream at the port of Vancouver waiting for cargo, these ships having a capacity of over eight or ten thousand tons each.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I ask whether any of the Canadian merchant marine were awaiting there?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I did not stop to examine their teeth. There was also a tremendous growth in the United States shipping from all the ports from Seattle down to San Francisco and further south. To give you an idea of the importance of the establishment of Yarrows at Esquimalt, let me say that during the twelve months ending March 1st, 1924, 111 ships were repaired by them, having an aggregate tonnage of some 280,000. Twenty-five vessels occupied the dock, one of them for a period of two months, indicating that a large trade has already been built up at that point. Other vessels were turned away because the present dockage facilities are far too small for their accommodation. This trade is a very important one. I recall that during the war one ship occupied the dry-dock at Esquimalt for a period of five months, the bill for repairs on which amounted to nearly half a million dollars. Only Canadian workmen were used in that work. In the case of crippled ships it is necessary to have dockage at a very convenient point, and Esquimalt is particularly well suited for this purpose.
To give you an idea of how our live American friends are taking care of the dock
situation, I may point out that there are no less than sixteen floating and graving docks between Seattle and San Francisco as compared with our two docks in use at present and two on the British Columbia coast under construction. Is it not better to be able to provide the accommodation for these vessels so that the work on British and Canadian vessels may be done on the Canadian side by Canadian workmen? The late government deserve very great credit for their farsightedness in commencing the construction of, proper docking facilities at the port of Esquimalt.
The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), when in opposition, objected very seriously indeed to the building of the Ballan-tyne pier at Vancouver, stating that it was an extravagant expenditure, that it was quite unnecessary, and that it would not be occupied for years. What is the situation now? The whole of the accommodation is taken up. This Ballantyne pier is rendering very valuable service, and I am quite sure that the Minister of Justice has seen the error that he made, and particularly at the time he had the honour of opening that pier amidst the popping of champagne corks. In fact my Liberal friends have always been rather slow to appreciate the great development on the Pacific coast. They object to the construction of the Esquimalt drydock, which I think I shall prove in a few moments to your entire satisfaction is a very timely piece of work indeed.
They have objected very sterenuously to the building of the Ballantyne pier. They even objected to the construction of the Canadian Pacific railway and some of their leaders of that day got up in the House and said: "This line will never earn its axle grease. Where is it going? It is only going to British Columbia, where there is nothing but a sea of mountains." In spite of those statements, and in spite of the fact that the country has been handicapped by Liberal governments since that time, the Canadian Pacific has made good and to-day it is one of the greatest transportation organizations in the world. However, as we say in the racing game, the Liberals are only riding to form in connection with the Esquimalt drydock when they object to its construction. I want to predict to my Liberal friends that before very many years it will be found that the dockage facilities on the Pacific coast are inadequate. If the increase in shipping proceeds at the rate at which it is going at the present time, I am quite sure we will not have to wait very long for that day.
The Address-Mr. Tolmie

Our friend the correspondent for MacLean's Magazine also takes violent objection to the location of this dock. Now, while it has always been recognized that he possessed a good deal of ability as a correspondent, I have never been informed that his services have been in demand as an expert on the location of drydocks. As a matter of fact, Esquimalt is very well located for drydock purposes. Situated on the Straits of Juan de Fuca, fifty miles from the Pacific on that arm of the sea through which every ship bound for southern British Columbia ports and for Puget Sound ports in the state of Washington must pass within a distance of twenty miles, this port is almost fog-free during the whole year, so that it is readily accessible at all times. The rainfall is very light indeed. The temperature at that port will run probably about 42 in winter time and about 60 in summer, with about five-and-a-half or six hours sunshine daily, on the average, throughout the year, enabling the workmen to work outside on these ships without the least inconvenience and without any artificial heating such as is necessary in eastern yards.
Situated from the Columbia river north to about the middle of the west coast of Vancouver Island, and covering the entrance to the Straits of Juan de Fuca, is what is known as the Graveyard of the Pacific. There is a tremendous current that sets in from the Pacific ocean to that coast. This current varies a great deal, and sometimes it attains a speed of five miles an hour. In thick weather vessels attempting to make these straits are affected by this current and frequently carried to the Vancouver Island coast and wrecked. I think I am safe in saying that more wrecks have occurred in that particular neighbourhood from the Columbia river north to the point I have mentioned than on any other part of the Pacific coast. Esquimalt is situated about eighty or ninety miles closer than any other drydock on the Canadian or American mainland, so the dry-dock is very conveniently situated for the ships in the event of their getting into trouble.
Esquimalt has long been recognized as a very central point. In very early days when the Hudson's Bay Company decided to locate in southern British Columbia and give up the territory lying north of the Columbia river to the Straits of Juan de Fuca, they had the selection of all the ports in western Canada, but they decided to establish one of their principal ports at Victoria and Esquimalt. Then when the. British navy was looking for a location on the Pacific coast, after giving the place a thorough looking over, they also decided on Esquimalt as the most 
appropriate place for a naval station. Then Yarrows, Limited, one of the largest shipbuilding firms in the world, located there, and to give you an idea of the size of that firm, in four years of the war they constructed no less than 58 war vessels, all of which were put into commission and stayed on top of the water, which is quite a different record to that made by some other shipbuilding concerns during the war. There can be no question, I think, as to whose argument should be accepted in favour of the location of this particular drydock, either the experts of Yarrows, Limited, engineers of long experience and specialists in that particular line, or the correspondent for MacLean's Magazine.
There has been an attempt made, I am sorry to say, by some members of the government during their meanderings over -the western provinces last summer to make political capital out of the building of this drydock. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) at Victoria had no criticisms to offer of this drydock at all. In a very pleasant way, and with a bland smile, he said there should be unity in Canada, that we should travel together shoulder to- shoulder to make this a great country, that there should be no Easterners and no Westerners, no Frenchspeaking and no English-speaking, but all one for the unity of Canada and for the building up of this country. This was all very excellent sentiment, but the good people of Victoria were impressed with his inconsistency. They could not understand how he would preach unity at the Pacific coast without preaching it in his own native province of Quebec, particularly, say, during the election of 1921. They could not understand why he with his associates during the election in Kent had preached anything but unity, in fact, why they had made efforts, to create racial prejudice for the purpose of getting votes. But when the Minister of Justice reached the prairies about a thousand miles from the sea, where the ozone from the Pacific did not permeate his nostrils any more, where the people did not know much about drydocks, and where he thought he was absolutely safe, his bland smile faded and with an indignant snort he announced that the previous government had built the drydock at Esquimalt for the purpose of electing Doctor Tolmie. He knew much better because he sat in the House here at the time this whole matter was discussed. But here was an opportunity, when he was safely away from the sea, and where nobody knew much about drydocks, where it would be difficult even to find a man who knew a drydock was something to put a ship into or

The Address-Mr. Tolmie
to tie it up to, to make such statements. He saw a chance there to attack the drydock and the previous government and he could not resist the opportunity.
The right hon. the Prime Minister, speaking in this debate, made statements that I was very sorry to see him make. I was sorry that he did not obtain as full information as possible before he touched upon this subject. A private member on the government or the opposition side can take a chance occasionally, but we look to ministers of the Crown to set an example to the whole House. Let us return to the days of the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier, a man whose name was respected from one end of this country to the other, a man whose ability was recognized and whose honesty of purpose was never doubted, a man who filled his position with dignity and who hesitated to make an inaccurate statement, a man who was fair in debate and who encouraged his associates to follow his example-compare this, if comparison is possible, with the example set by the two hon. members to whom I have just referred. Further, when we take into consideration the history of broken pledges, when we take into consideration the history of misrepresentations that have been going on since 1921, we must realize how the mighty have fallen and how a once great party in Canada has degenerated. On coming into power in 1921 the present government stopped the operations at Esquimalt for a period of several months. This incurred heavy damages from the contractors, and it is generally accepted at the coast that it was entirely unnecessary. Everyone knows that with the efficient Public Works department in operation, with their engineers actually on the ground watching every move of the contractors, that any information regarding the construction of the work could have been obtained within a few hours and this serious delay-throwing a large number of working people out of work and at the same time incurring a very heavy extra expenditure-would have been unnecessary. I want to say that the Minister of Public Works, in contrast to his colleagues and with a more particular knowledge of conditions on the Pacific coast, was manly enough to state that this dock was not only a good work but should have been commenced in 1912. Therefore I appreciate the action he took in this connection. That is all I have to say, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the drydock situation. I want to close by stating frankly that we have not got any more dock accommodation on the Pacific coast than is going to be necessary, and I think the late government deserves great credit for their foresight 28
in being able to look into the future, the same as Yarrows Limited, and taking measures to promote the great prosperity of the Coast.
The Minister of Justice in his speech on March 14, referred to the construction of four wooden barquentines in the city of Vancouver, and pointed to the gross extravagance of the late government in building these ships. Here again one is struck with the partial statement of facts. I am prepared to tell the story clearly and fully to this House and through this House to the people of Canada and let the case stand on its merits. In the first place the contract for these ships was not let in 1919, as stated by the Minister of Justice, but on March 16, 1920. He did not say a word about the desperate unemployment conditions that existed at the Pacific coast at that time. These ships were primarily constructed to meet that very serious situation which existed in British Columbia during 1919 and 1920. It will be remembered that when demobilization took place the returned soldifers were offered a chance to demobilize in any part of the country they wished. The result was that a very large number went out to the Pacific coast and were demobilized there. In consequence there were thousands of returned men on the Pacific coast, many thousands more than had enlisted in the province, greatly increasing the unemployment situation. The lumbermen of British Columbia, noticing the success of lumber carrying in wooden sailing ships, had long argued that if sailing ships were available they could convey lumber from British Columbia to distant ports of the world at very small expense. In the case of one of these barquentines such as was built at Victoria the crew numbered only fifteen or sixteen men, the carrying capacity would be around 2,000,000 feet of lumber, and, without any fuel being necessary, the transportation of lumber was done at the lowest possible cost, providing a reasonable trip was made. On looking round for some means of employment for the returned soldiers out of work it was decided that wooden ship construction offered the very best opportunities to provide the most work for the greatest number of men. In the first place work would be necessary in the woods in getting out the logs. Then it would be necessary to transport these logs to the sawmill, where work was provided for the men in the cutting up of the logs. Then followed the transfer of the cut timber to the ship yards where the returned men could take part in the building of the ships. So there was no other particular line of work offered as much opportunity for employment as the

The Address-Mr. Tolmie

construction of the wooden ship at that time. Strong pressure was brought to bear on the government by returned men and others at that period, and finally a delegation consisting of returned men, labour representatives, and merchants, headed by the mayor of the city of Victoria, came here in December, 1919, and urged the government to undertake the construction of these ships. The government refused to build ships on their own account, but after a while a compromise was reached whereby a company was to be created in the city of Victoria. They were to subscribe a certain amount of the money, and the government was to advance the balance needed for the construction of each vessel at 6 per cent interest, and to have a first mortgage on the finished ship. Some six hundred of Victoria's citizens co-operated with a view of helping out the situation and doing something towards getting the returned men re-established. In the contract a clause was inserted making it necessary to employ not less than 60 per cent of returned men, and every man was to be hired through the government labour bureau. Due to the men being new at the work- many of them having had no previous experience in ship building-and also due to a lack of capital, the project did not turn out successfully, with the result that only one ship was finished. She turned out very well and conveyed several cargoes of lumber to the distant ports of the world. Finally the ship got into a very severe hurricane in the southern seas, had to put into the port of Honolulu for repairs, and on her return to Victoria was disposed of by the government. The other ships were partially finished, the hull of one being about half done, another one fairly well advanced, and the keel of the third one, I think laid. When this government came into power it required from December, 1921, to October 3, 1923, to wind up the affairs of this company, almost two years. During this period there was a very serious loss incurred from the deterioration of material of various kinds but had this matter been handled in a more businesslike manner by the Minister of Justice, who was then Minister of Marine, many thousands of dollars would have been saved. I may say that the shareholders lost all their money in connection with this venture. There were several organizations, such as returned soldiers' bodies, that offered to take hold of these yards, but no bargain could be made with them. The Minister of Justice quoted a letter from Mr. Ballan-tyne addressed to me in which it was stated that he would take no interest in the construction of these ships. Let me say that 
during the whole period of the construction of the vessels the work was carried on under the supervision of the Department of Marine, Mr. Ballantyne's department, which maintained a man on the ground to supervise the work.
Let me point out too, Mr. Speaker, that the present Labour government in Great Britain to meet the existing labour situation there which is aggravated, but which is no
9 p.m. worse than the situation on the Pacific coast at the time I mention, have recently let a contract for the building of five cruisers. The British government do not really need the vessels, they are building them simply to meet the existing situation. I claim that the late government in Canada followed the only course it was possible to follow in the construction of these wooden barquentines and in undertaking other work on the Pacific coast to provide for the unemployment, and that this was ten times better than the adoption of the dole system which has very bad results on our working people.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I have no further remarks to make in this connection. I only hope that I have made my explanations concerning these two ventures very clear to the House.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
It has
been gratifying to me, Sir, and to some of us in this part of the House, that the present debate has turned almost entirely on the tariff question. Old political prophets such as Cartwright and Blake foresaw this day. They knew it had to come. They said it would take more than a generation for the people of this country to wake up to the position they were placed in by the Old National Policy. It has taken more than a generation, but the day has come, and this question has got to be settled first. The trade penalty known us the tariff, is a tax that must be paid by a class who receive no benefit from it. In the case of Canada it is chiefly the farmer who pays because he is not able to pass on the unjust charge to any other class, and he can no longer bear the burden. Every advocate of trade penalties in this House during this debate has drawn an awful picture of what is going to happen to Canada if the tariff is abolished or even lowered. But they have not even deigned to notice the state of agriculture as it is to-day. That state has been brought about by the tariff during the years since the National Policy was first inaugurated. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) has stated that the reference to the

The Address-Mr. Evans
tariff in the Speech is like the sword of Damocles hanging by a single thread, a slender thread, over the heads of the manufacturers. He declares that they cannot purchase their raw material without a proper interpretation of what this means. The inference is that they must have a privilege maintained or go out of business. But one thing which has appeared. very striking to me, Sir, during the whole of this debate, is that those who have taken part in this discussion and advocate protection, look upon it, not as a concession, but as an inherent right. But there has never been anything in this House before that has so nonplussed the manufacturers as the inference in the Speech from the Throne tnat the Liberal party is coming back to its own platform. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) indulges in his usual accusation of the density of mind of myself and my colleagues here, and indeed he almost despairs of penetrating that density in his plea for the manufacturers, in propounding the old joke of a home market. To me, Sir, the incongruity would seem to be that the hon. member is trying to elucidate a theory which the Romans four thousand years ago found to be a fallacy. That was when for a time the slave dealers of that period were successful in getting the ear of their government, The hon. member says at page 304 of Hansard-
I must be most weak in placing my argument if I cannot make myself clearly understood.
I wish to inform the hon. gentleman, since it is evident he does not know, that there is no logical argument for class privilege, or as he would call it protection. At best it is an imposition, it is a trade penalty, and in the end is bound to prove a boomerang even to those for whose benefit it was first inaugurated. Even on the hon. gentleman's own admission, which I do not admit myself, the woollen industry is in a serious condition, a most hopeless condition, after enjoying for 40 years this privilege of extracting from the home consumer at least one-third of their income, for which they have given nothing in return. No one can deny that the consumers of this country have paid one-third more for their woollen goods than they could have been bought for in the markets of the world. According to reports the Canadian Manufacturers' Association held a meeting at Hamilton on January 24th. It was devoted almost entirely to the tariff. Since then, I believe, they have been presenting demands to the government here for increased import penal-28i
ties. Now, the manufacturers have had protection since 1879, and since that time they have obtained privileges such as the manufacturers in other countries never dreamed of. They pleaded then for privileges because they were infant industries. They have abused these privileges. They have destroyed their own market. And now, like the dope fiend, they come back for more of the stuff that has brought them to this state of imbecility. The report of the special committee of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association on taxation is perhaps the most illogical product of biased minds imaginable; and the resolution previously passed, and again reaffirmed at that meeting is almost ridiculous, to say the least, as it declares that the adoption of a stable and sound fiscal policy based on an adequate customs tariff will bind together more firmly the provinces of Canada in national unity. The report declares that this policy will attract capital, commercialize our natural resources, strengthen existing industries, and create new industries:	raise
revenue, encourage immigration, provide employment, increase traffic for the railways and for our national ports, lower freight rates and make farming profitable, create new markets abroad and facilitate profitable bargaining by means of tariffs with other countries. Well, everybody is to be made rich and happy. Producers and consumers alike are to be benefited simply by the process of reducing imports or prohibiting imports, the government is to reap an increased revenue from a diminished source-most remarkable. A protective tariff cannot benefit every citizen alike. If it did it would not be protection at all. And the fact tin-' Canadian manufacturers have benefited is because they have charged an unjust price, a price not based at all on competition for their goods which the home consumer must pay Without going into the whole question and answering all the statements in that resolution, I want to say that protection does not increase employment and importation does not lessen it. Why? Because all imports must be paid for by exports.
In this connection, I was surprised to hear the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) declaim against the evil of spending $1.50 in the United States for every dollar they buy from us. This is an old argument, and to some extent in the past our people have believed that an evil did exist in the fact. But what are the real facts? The protectionist is equally averse to the importation of goods from Great Britain even though
The Address-Mr. Evans

from the application of the dumping clause. The words "fair value for home consumption" are no longer impartially interpreted; they are interpreted according to who the importer happens to be. It is not the business of any government to discriminate between one citizen and another; the laws of the country should be the same for all. I say these words are interpreted according to who the importer happens to be, and no co-operative concern can buy for co-operative distribution anywhere in Canada. They cannot get their supplies without being penalized under the antidumping clause. If anything is done at this session to lighten the load which at present bears upon the farmer of this country, it should be to abolish the anti-dumping clause. Of course if anything worth while is done it will be a general cut on the whole list so that the cost of living may be brought down to a lower level. But the anti-dumping clause as it stands to-day and as it is being applied today is the one thing that stands in the way of any co-operative effort of the people themselves to lower the cost of living.
The agriculturist has borne pretty well the whole burden. I fancy I can hear hon. gentlemen say that if we abolish the anti-dumping clause we shall be overwhelmed with goods from Germany, from the United States, and perhaps from some other countries. I want to tell this House that the agriculturists of this country can stand a good deal of dumping at the present time. People on the farms to-day are short of every commodity they need, but the distributing combine, which, according to the president of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, is sixty per cent too great in number, is so completely organized so far as this anti-dumping provision is concerned that they have got the prices too high to permit our people to purchase the goods they need, even after marketing the biggest crop in the history of this country. Our purchasing power has been destroyed through the operation of the anti-dumping clause and this condition will prevail as long as certain interests are protected by these measures. We sell our produce in line with the world's prices, after having to raise it under these conditions.
Coming to a remark made by the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) regarding the percentages of increases of our products, and of our commodities. I wish to correct him in one or two particulars. He says that the price of one or two of our chief products increased in 1923 over the 1913 price by 51 per cent. It is not so. Taking his own figures which he himself gives, the increase works out at 28 per cent, and not at

51 per cent as stated by him. The hon. gentleman may not have meant to create that impression, but an error of 23 per cent is rather too much to go uncorrected. Then again, on four of our chief products he says there is an increase of 44 per cent. Again taking his own figures, we find that the increase is not 44 per cent but 35 per cent. I am rer ferring to the figures he gave as found on page 311 of Hansard.
Although there are hard times in Canada to-day, I am not one of those who would write "Ichabod" over the portals of this nation. But I do want to give notice to some of those who are responsible for the policy of this country, financial and industrial, and who are responsible for the present conditions of life on the farms as well as in the centres of industry, that they have no right to saddle themselves on the backs of the workers, whether farmers or labourers. This nation needs a whole course of civic and national instruction, but at present it seems that our schools and colleges are muzzled by privilege. Our moneyed magnates and industrial kings are simply goading men into rebellion, and they have these measures to protect them. Let us treat men as men, and a display of the militia with their bayonets and rifles will not be needed to preserve order The working man of this nation, whether the farmer or the labourer, must be given his share, he must have his rights recognized. And when men are given their rights they willingly assume the responsibilities of citizenship. To this end the cost of living must be no longer burdened with trade penalties, and the efforts and enterprises of the people individual and co-operative, must not be held down by any class privilege.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that I shall receive the gratitude of my associates-of my word weary associates, I might say-when I announce that I am not going to say a word about the tariff. It is a great temptation, I admit, but I have steeled my heart and my conscience and I am not going to say a word more about it I only want to speak for a few minutes about some remarks that fell from the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie). He reproached the cabinet benches, more particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), I think, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), warning them that whatever we might expect from the common herd of members, at least from the cabinet, from men of their position, we expected a measure of fairness and truth in their pronouncements. Surely that was a very modest statement, I

The Address-Mr. Neill
hope, Sir; the standard of our Canadian statesmanship as exemplified by ordinary common members is not so low as to cause us not to expect some measure of fairness and truth even from the common herd. However, he confines it entirely to the demand that those on the front government benches shall have some measure of truth and fairness in their utterances. I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if that is also extended to ex-cabinet ministers? I recall some months ago an ex-cabinet minister coming-shall I say, returning?-to British Columbia, after a careful and no doubt thoughtful and thorough survey of the political conditions of Canada, and, like all politicians, when he came home he told us what his reasoned judgment was as to those conditions. He told us that in the election, which he said was imminent, Quebec was going to return a large number of Conservatives. He told us that Nova Scotia, as evidenced by the recent by-elections there, would be probably solid Conservative. Ontario was going to tell the same glad tale, but it was when he came to the prairies that his enthusiasm fairly boiled over; he said that the Progressive party was breaking up and flocking in large numbers to the Conservative standard. I cannot imitate to the full the beauty of his language, but' it gave the impression of a mighty ice-bound river breaking up and the people who had been caught on the ice making all possible attempts to reach the haven of rescue which he described as being within the Conservative party. He gave us the impression that it would be like the children of Israel who, after they had been bitten by serpents, had only to look to the brazen serpent to their right and all would be well. Curiously enough he did not tell us anything about what was going to happen in British Columbia, because we might know what is going to happen there. It is noble to seek truth, Mr. Speaker; it is beautiful to find it, is it not?
Before I pass on to what I really want to speak about, and that is the drydock, I would like to say a few words about the question of wooden ships or ships of any kind that were built during the war in Victoria. I am sorry that any man from British Columbia has raised that question here to-night, for it is one that none of us who know the circumstances can recall with anything but reproach. I know something, a very little, of the way those ships were built, and what I do know gives part of the reason why we are paying such enormous taxes to-day. Graft was rampant in every detail in the manner in which they were built. I had a friend who went there
to work. He was a carpenter, employed in putting in panels, and he wanted to hold his job. Poor foolish man, he thought that working was a necessity to hold his job, and he started to put in his best licks. Along about eleven o'clock the straw boss came along and asked, "How many panels have you put in?" He spoke harshly, and the carpenter thought he was finding fault. "I have only put in five," he said, "but I guess I can put in another before noon, and once I get in my stride I will do better than that." "Good Lord, man" was the reply, "do you know what is a day's work here on these panels? Five panels is a day's work, and don't you put in another panel to-day." That is an absolute fact, recorded by a man who was there. Another man told me that his greatest difficulty was to keep out of sight. That was all he was asked to do. He registered when he went in and again when he came out, and all he had to do in the meantime was to keep out of sight. Those are facts perfectly well known on the Pacific coast, and it ill becomes any man from British Columbia to talk about the scandal connected with the building of ships in Victoria. I would not have mentioned this if it had not been forced upon me.
My hon. friend began his remarks, very much to my surprise, by a criticism of the articles appearing in MacLean's Magazine. I was very much surprised because I thought the general trend of those articles was distinctly favourable to the party of my hon. friend. If I recall correctly the very first article ended with a recommendation to turn the present government out of power. You would think that was more or less of a partisan statement, and I think the trend all through has been somewhat similar. Now my hon. friend finds fault with these articles and with the man who wrote them, but his views are not shared by the remainder of his party. In MacLean's Magazine of March 1st I find two pages of eulogies from various prominent statesmen, politicians and newspapers. One is from Mr. George B. Jones, M.P. who writes, "I feel sure the criticism will do good, and we do know that it is truthful." Then we have Senator Gideon D. Robertson giving the articles his blessing. We find also the Hon. H. H. Stevens, of Vancouver, giving them his blessing. How'are the mighty fallen from their seats! There is also a whole page of eulogies from newspapers. I do not know them all, but the British Columbia ones which I do know, are distinctly Conservative in their attitude, so my friend in finding fault with the writer is going contrary to the traditions of his party, which is generally all to stick together.
The Address-Mr. Neill

He has told us a great deal about the need of a drydock. He told us how a certain portion of the Pacific ocean is known as the graveyard of the Pacific, and he drew some kind of analogy that the one needed the other, But you do not need drydocks to rescue ships, not at all. After a boat has gone on that west coast there is very little hope for it. If it is pulled off it will be pulled off by a wrecking crew and a ship adapted for that purpose. It would be towed to the drydock; you could not tow the drydock to the ship. So all this talk about the west coast and the graveyard of the Pacific has nothing at all to do with the point. I failed to hear, but that might have been my misfortune, two years ago and again last year when I was in this House beseeching the Minister of Marine to take the necessary steps for properly safeguarding that graveyard-I failed to find my hon. friend with all his local knowledge and with his position as an ex-cabinet minister lending the weight of his great influence to my representations. But to the honour of the minister those improvements were for the most part put in order, and to that it can be ascribed that there have been very few wrecks there since then. One small addition alone, that of the direction-finding machine at Pachena, has been the means of saving several ships this winter. In the month of December alone they had seven hundred calls, which they answered. Of course, many of them were from ships just testing their position, but in many cases this improvement has saved valuable ships from going on the rocks, and that is far more use than this drydock after you have got it on the rocks.
But the point made by my hon. friend was that the Prime Minister in his opening speech made the statement that this drydock was built to elect the hon. gentleman. The Prime Minister did not tell us it was not a dry-dock or should not be a drydock, he said the drydock was built to elect the ex-Minister of Agriculture, and I will endeavour to show how much of that is true. By the way, in his closing remarks the hon. member said that this drydock was going to be necessary. There are a lot of things going to be necessary, but we do not spend five millions on them before they do become necessary.
The Prime Minister said that the drydock was built to elect the hon. member. Victoria, I am sorry to say, although I am not a native of that city, has always been a city that was peculiarly susceptible to invitations, we will call it, of that character. It always needed a hand-out in plain English. That is one of the reasons perhaps we find that the

representation in parliament from rural constituencies is-I will not say a cleaner body- but a less approachable body than those from the cities. You could bribe one big city with a drydock or with a great many other things, but you cannot bribe a whole agricultural community, because the little town that gets the graft will be vehemently opposed by all the other little towns. But in the case of a city like Victoria they look for, and generally get, a hand-out of some description. Far back in the history of British Columbia politics I can recall when railway charters were the order of the day. The government then was practically a Victorian government. I always used to notice that it did not matter where the railway was projected, either in the extreme eastern part of British Columbia or elsewhere, so long as the terminus of the proposed railway was in the city of Victoria they could get a charter for their railway no matter how outrageous and unreasonable it was. So it has gone all down the line. I can recall two elections, because the government generally carry one on the promise and one on its tardy fulfilment, that the government won on the building of enormous expensive docks. Of course, the fact that they were unnecessary had nothing whatever to do with it. That was many years ago, and even to-day those great ocean docks are not connected with the railway. But that did not matter. They had to have the docks, and it was only after they were built-I do not know why, because there was so little shipping-that they discovered that the dock was four feet too high or four feet too low and that no large ocean-going boat could dock there, or ever will dock there for that reason. Twenty or thirty years ago members who come from the Old Country will recall that there was a great cry in magazine articles, "What shall we do with our boys?" The boys were growing up; the colonies were but little known then, and every other magazine had an article on, what shall we do with our boys? Very often they sent them to Canada, to the great benefit of this country. But in Victoria the question has arisen among the latter day statesmen: What shall we do with our docks? Various suggestions were made, but the brightest one came a few months ago when the tide of wheat began to flow into Vancouver. One man wrote a series of articles in the papers to prove that the proper thing was to ship the wheat from them. The wheat was to be brought to Vancouver and transported thence to Victoria then I presume carried by wagon from the terminus of the railway to the dock, to the docks that were four feet out of level, and then put into the

The Address-Mr. Neill
ship, and as the writer pathetically said, "It will be something to do with our docks." As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, and I think perhaps it is a good idea for every one to speak the truth on this matter, that drydock should have been built in Vancouver, and I defy the members for Vancouver, any one of them, to stand up in his place and contradict me. The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) went into facts and figures, and I am pleased to follow him. He said that? the drydock site was bought in the year 1913 or 1914 at a place called Lang's Cove. That is quite true, but there are some half truths that are worse than an absolute deception. I have no doubt that a site was bought. The sum of three or four hundred thousand dollars was spent, but the site was not worth anything because you could not make a dry dock there. Perhaps it was never intended to put one there. However it served to carry the election at that particular date. Later on came this other election, and it was felt that something really had to be done this time; the people would not stand putting off any longer and a drydock had to be built. However the dock was not built at Lang's Cove, it was built at Skinner's Cove. Now, the money was voted on the 27th June, 1919, that was five years after the false dock site was bought and found to be unsuitable. So they got busy. On the 27th June, 1919, the money was voted to go on with the dock, and on the 2nd August, the hon. member was sworn in as Minister of Agriculture. Could anyone see a connection between those two facts? On the previous occasion the site was bought at a place that was no good and the matter had not been touched for five long years, but at the crucial moment-not at the crucial moment, I am exaggerating, but five weeks before my hon. friend was sworn in, it was discovered that the site was not suitable. Another site was bought, and parliament voted the money to build this drydock. My hon. friend tells us further that half a million dollars was set aside out of that sum in July for boring to find out whether it was suitable or not, and he was sworn in on 2nd August of the same year. With true modesty my hon. friend merely told us that he was sworn in "some time after that".

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Will the hon. member
tell us who was Minister of Agriculture at the time the vote passed this House?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
No, but the hon. member
for Victoria was the expectant minister.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I tell the hon. gentleman that the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) was minister and there was no expectation whatever.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I do. not suppose the hon.
member for Marquette was instrumental in getting a vote for his successor.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
He was the member
of ,.the government who recommended it to this House.	[DOT]

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: On the advice of whom?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: On his own advice.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: On his own advice?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The hon. member for Marquette recommended a dry dock for Victoria on his own advice? Do I get that right?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
What I said, and I do
not propose to be misrepresented, was that he was the member of the government which recommended it. When the hon. member asked me upon whose advice he was a member of the government, I said, on his own advice.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I did not refer to the creation of the hon. member for Marquette, I was talking about the creation of the dry-dock, or rather the vote for the drydock.
Now, I propose with your permission, Mr. Speaker, to quote a few extracts, a very few, from the Victoria Colonist. Those who are familiar with it know that the Victoria Colonist is a strong Conservative paper, and therefore its absolute accuracy can be relied on.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Much better than yours.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If the hon. member wants
to speak I will be happy to yield him the floor.
On October 16, 1919,-by the way I may say that while the hon. member was sworn in on the 2nd August, 1919, the election was not held until October 27-that date is important; October 27. So we find on October 16 an editorial reading as follows:
The announcement is made that tenders for the dry-dock will be called for immediately.
That was eleven days before the election. Just about the psychological moment was it not? On the same date in the same paper at a meeting we find Hon. Dr. Tolmie speaking as follows:
They tell you that this drydock scheme is merely a vote catching one. Before I left Ottawa I had the definite assurance from members of the Cabinet that
The Address-Mr. Neill

this work will be proceeded with. I fully believe that assurance.
On October 19, we again find my hon. friend making the following statement:
As to the drydock there is no camouflage so far as I and the government are concerned. The government has given me its solemn pledge that the work will be proceeded with and I am here to say the work will go on.
You see he had to be emphatic because this was the second time the drydock had been undertaken. Then again, on October 21, in his printed manifesto to the electors my hon. friend used this language:
We secured a vote for it (the drydock) at end of June (1919) and work will be proceeded with without delay.
On October 26, as the final windup before the election, which was next day, we find an editorial reading as follows:
People will attest by their votes their estimate of how much Mr. Tolmie was responsible for having made it possible for this great shipping facility to be begun this winter.
And there are more with which I will not burden the House.
There is just one other point I wish to allude to. The hon. member (Mr. Tolmie) said in his speech, and so did the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Dickie) that, after all, Esqui-malt, where this dry dock is, is not in the district of Victoria but in that of Nanaimo. That is just one of these truths which is true but misleading. It is perfectly and literally correct that it is not within the actual confines of the district of Victoria, it is in that of Esquimalt which extends up to Nanaimo eighty or a hundred miles. But Esquimalt is, to all intents and purposes a suburb of Victoria about two and a half miles distant and connected with it by tram line. Citizens of Victoria live out that way in pretty villas, and so on. The working people of Victoria go out there to work and vice versa. They are one and the same to all intents and 10 p.m. purposes. The expenditure of $5,000,000 in Esquimalt would accomplish as much benefit and be as successful in vote getting in the city of Victoria as a like expenditure in Ottawa would be in the city of Hull; the parable is an exact one. While it is perfectly true it is in the Nanaimo district, yet to all intents and purposes the benefit and the vote catching value of it would be just the same as if it were in the actual city of Victoria. Truth is a noble thing. Truth is supposed to be at the bottom of wells, but some wells are very deep.
Now the text of my hon. friend's eloquence was directed towards the statement of the
Prime Minister that the drydock was built to 
ensure his election. I maintain that I have sufficiently demonstrated the facts to hon. members to make up their minds. As to whether the Prime Minister was correct in that assertion I will leave it to them to say-I recall that some years ago, in the time of the great boom there was an intensive campaign to advertise motor cars throughout the States. One man advertised: "This is the best car." A second advertised: "This is the cheapest car." A third man sai4: "This is the safest;" and so on. But one particular man thought he knew the mind of the American people, thought he knew the class of people to whom he was appealing, and he advertised his car with these words: "This is the dearest car." He knew his clientele; he was out to catch the purse-proud millionaire who wanted to be able to say: "My car cost more than anybody else's." So we find a parallel to-day in the case of my hon. friend. He goes about the country a great deal, during the parliamentary recess, engaged in a business which is a sort of collateral to his political duties, and he will be able to point to himself as "a pearl of great price." I remember that when Paul was haled before-was it not Agrippa?-in the course of his trial it came out that he was a Roman citizen, a great honour in those days. The chief captain looked at him and asked how he came to be that. Paul said, Yes, he was a Roman citizen, and the chief captain replied, "With a great sum obtained I this." So my hon. friend can say "With a great sum obtained I this seat." But the commoner, the ordinary members from the prairies and other districts, can perhaps say, like Paul, "But we were free born."

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I wish to deal briefly with the remarks of the hon. member for Comox-A-lberni (Mr. Neill), but before doing so I wish to express my regret as a young man'-and I am sure many hon. gentlemen feel the same way-at the absence of one of our Canadian statesmen, the Minister of Finance, the member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding). We all miss him in this House. We miss the brilliancy of his mind and the soundness of his judgment. I had not anticipated making any references to the remarks of the last speaker, but he has hurled at me and my colleagues from Vancouver a defy regarding the Esquimalt drydock. He says that he defies the members from Vancouver to contradict the assertion that a drydock should have been built at Vancouver. Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to deny this assertion and say that a drydock should have been built at Esquimalt, but may I add, as actually happened, another

The Address-Mr. Ladner
should have been built at Vancouver. I was much interested, really more interested, in the fact that the hon. member rose in this House for the first time as a champion of the government. He is the man selected to answer perhaps the most popular member of this House, the hon. member for Victoria City, and he seeks to throw ridicule upon him, invective, and to charge him with insincerity. Any hon. member who knows the hon. member for Victoria City knows perfectly well that none of those allegations could be applied to him, and these remarks, coming from an hon. member and a gentleman who for many years has known the reputation of such a distinguished member of this House as the hon. member for Victoria City, are somewhat surprising to me. I would have thought perhaps the government would have chosen someone from some other portion of the country to have performed this kind of deed, let me say, to use parliamentary language. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni reminds me of the experience of a friend of mine who was travelling from New York over to a great convention of Rotarians in Edinburgh, and, as many of you know, each Rotarian carries the badge on the lapel of his coat, with his name, place of residence and occupation. On one beautiful Sunday morning a certain serious-minded,-should	I say long-facedindividual, proceeded about the boat, and without any explanation or without any words whatever, he would come to one member after the other, take hold of the lapel of the coat, and examine the badge with a magnifying glass. My friend proceeded with his reading, but soon this individual found his way to him, and the friend suddenly saw a large hand appear under his nose which hand grabbed the lapel of his coat adjusted the magnifying glass and examined the badge. The gentleman looked up in great surprise and this is what the man said: "I am Alex. Smith of Spokane undertaker; I am looking for somebody". The double application of the story rather fits the present situation. The hon. gentleman has endeavoured to answer the hon. member for Victoria City with arguments and assertions, which are witty, but which are not nearly so substantial, and not nearly so sound in fact as the assertion we have heard from the hon. member for Victoria.
Before proceeding with the main portion of my remarks I would like-and it is with a little diifidemce I undertake this duty-to refer to the words of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) this afternoon. That hon. member is generally fairly accurate, but
to-day he launched into a torrent of political argument, no doubt for political effect, with regard to a certain statement made by Mr. Monty at Montreal. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that although the Minister of Railways may be good in the administration of his department he was a little bit out in his French, not that I profess any excellent knowledge of French, but I have special means of knowing something about it. The actual words which were published in the press on Tuesday, the 29th January, 1921 were as follows-
Les liberaux, dit M. Monty, n'ont pas tenu parole; its avaient formellement declare que les chemins de fer nationaux seraient remis a une compagnie privee; au lieu de cela, on destitue les commissaires et on fait venir un etranger pour les administrer.
Now, Mr. Speaker, for the interpretation of those words I have not only my own authority but, the authority of one more skilled in interpretation than I am. The interpretation of that word "etranger" literally means stranger, not in the sense of meaning foreigner, but someone outside our gates. The French language is full of delicacies and sentiment which I am afraid most of the Anglo-Saxon race do nut appreciate.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Give us the whole quotation, because we require to hear the whole of it to understand its significance.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman's
French is in working order to-night he will have understood it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Read the English version of it.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The interpretation of it
would be-
"The Liberals," said Mr. Monty, "did not keep their word. They formally declared that the National Railways would be returned to private ownership, instead of which they dismissed the directors and had a stranger appointed to administer them."
A foreigner and an alien would be a different individual in sentiment and warmth of feeling, from an ordinary stranger. There is that line of demarcation on which the Minister of Railways in his characteristic, witty and skilful manner has seen fit to take a political advantage of ^nd make a great fuss over, so that the newspapers would have a Lord Dundonald case i'll over again.
Most of the discussion in this House has been directed to the question of tariff. We have heard advocates cf tariff and more tariff. We have heard advocates of duties and less duties, and, if I remember my history cor-
The Address-Mr. Ladner

rectly, I think for the past 70 years public men have been advocating the pros and cons of the principles of free trade and protection without giving actual practical application of those principles to the conditions of the country as we find them. I was reading the other day in the Life of Sir Alexander Galt, a speech which he made in the House in 1850, when he was raising the duty from 7i to 10 per cent, and in that speech he was remarking on the disaster that would fall upon the United States because they had such high duties. I think they were 25 per cent, and he had it skilfully worked out that people would' leave the United States because the cost of living would go up and they would come to Canada. He used the very arguments which hon. members to my left are advancing, which arguments have been proven in the light of history to be absolutely without foundation.
I propose to say a few words with respect to the portion of the Speech from the Throne dealing with the question of banking. The Speech from the Throne says-
The amendments made to the Bank Act in the last decennial revision of the last session provided better guarantees for the public in banking operations; their wisdom has already been abundantly apparent.
I suppose the wisdom which has already been abundantly apparent may be found in the disaster of the Home Bank, as to which some hon. members of the government have had some information. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that although the Banking Committee sat three and a half months, and took a great amount of evidence, which, with the report covers 1,060 pages; yet the government, in the full possession of a number of facts which I shall disclose to the House, made scarcely any changes in the act, in the face of a situation which is becoming inimical to the best interests of the country and of our banking institutions. The banks constitute the heart of our economic system. Our agriculture, our industry, our business generally, all live or die under that, system. To continue the parallel, money is the life blood of the economic state; and so long as the heart of the economic system pulsates normally and distributes that life blood properly throughout the whole economic being, the national health will be maintained in vigour and be able to carry all the burdens of war and taxation which bear down on the shoulders of this virile northern race. The banking question is not a very complicated one. The functions which the banks discharge are simple. They are to receive the savings of depositors subject to repayment on demand, and to act

as a medium for loaning those moneys to the business of the country. Banks, like other businesses, must take their chances; the shareholders and creditors must take a certain amount of risk. For nearly one hundred years parliament has seen fit, in the public interest, to make laws respecting our banks, and our banking institutions have performed a splendid service in this country. There is no question about that; in fact, I think we have one of the best banking systems in the world. Like all good systems, however, the banking system in Canada is capable of improvement, and I hope to demonstrate this in a few moments. With respect to the Committee on Banking and Commerce and its report, the responsibility lay primarily on the government. What did they do as a matter of fact? Briefly, these are the accomplishments. They restricted the loans to bank officials. They made a change in the form of monthly returns, but with little improvement. Amendments were made to make more effective the shareholders' audit and to give greater power to the minister to investigate the banks. The trouble, however, is that the powers which the minister has in that regard are generally not exercised until after the failure has occurred or until some catastrophe has overtaken the institution.
The most important change was the amendment in connection with the famous section 88, under which the Dominion banks advance moneys to business concerns and have a first charge on the goods. The government proposed-and it was inserted in the bill-to add section 8S (a), by which notice of intention to borrow is filed with the Receiver General for the express purpose of giving notice to the public of the existence of a charge against these particular goods of the business. The real truth is that this amendment, pretending to be in the interests of the public and of our business institutions, was nothing more nor less than a sham, because it was a very simple matter for a man to borrow under section 88, file his notice, order his goods from England and then borrow again under section 86, repaying what he got under section 88, cancelling the notice under section 88 (a), and then standing before the world as though his goods were not encumbered, whereas, in fact, they would be just as much encumbered as they were before. It was not from any lack of information that the government pursued that course. An expert witness from Great Britain explained the matter, as can be seen by reference to the Banking Committee's report. Yet the government pursued that policy, which was fair neither to the public nor to the

The Address-Mr. Ladner
business institutions. In fact, it was deceiving ; and business men will easily carry on their affairs under that amendment believing that there are no encumbrances against particular goods when in fact there may be. What is it that the government have failed to do? They have failed to grapple properly with the question of rural credits. Years ago when the banking institutions were first started in this country their purpose was as we see in the preamble to the bill incorporating the Bank of Montreal in 1817, namely, to use the words of this preamble:
The advancement of agriculture and commerce and the promotion of the prosperity of the province.
What a change has come over the institution of banking in one hundred years! We know to-day that banking is adapted to the commerce and industry of the country; short term loans are made covering periods of sixty, ninety and a hundred and twenty days, and money which is loaned over a longer period-investment money-is placed usually in long term bonds and mortgages for three and five year terms. But there is nothing to enable the farmer to secure a loan for nine, twelve or fifteen months. In that respect the last decennial revision of the Bank Act failed to grapple with the problem of rural credits, and nothing has been accomplished; no step has been taken to stop the absorption by the larger banks of the smaller ones, I will deal with that phase of the matter in a few moments.
Then we have the extraordinary situation in connection with the small amount of capital which is carrying an immense amount of deposits of the people. And nothing was done with regard to excessive rates of interest. I know that you cannot legislate on the question of interest rates, but steps can be taken to make impossible such incidents as were disclosed before the committee where on loans an interest of 10 and 12 per cent, was charged farmers in remote sections of Saskatchewan. Then, again, in connection with audit and inspection, it is well known that the government has not accomplished anything of advantage. They made certain amendments but they do not solve the question. It is generally understood that the government will probably provide some measure this session, but nothing satisfactory has been accomplished so far. There is also the question of penalties for false or incorrect returns. These penalties do not attach to the officials of the institution in the way they should in order to bring home the responsibility when such a catastrophe occurs as happened in the case of the Home Bank. Let me add that these are not dark
and mysterious questions which cannot be investigated nor understood. The history of the development of banking and financial institutions in Canada discloses the fact that time and again problems have arisen before the Banking committee and solutions have been suggested, tried and failed. In that respect the government, I think, have failed entirely to fix the responsibility, and they have not solved the problem as they should have done.
May I now direct the attention of the House concretely to some of the very important indications of the general tendency of events to-day. After all, the course of events to-day is merely a connection between the past and the future. I have obtained certain information from the returns given by our banks under the Bank Act and published in the Canada Gazette. In 1867 there were 22 banks in Canada; in 1890 there were 40, affording a wide field for competition. In 1900 there were 36, in 1910, 28, and in 1923 the number had been reduced to 14. What will the number be in 1933? If this does not indicate the trend of events, let me call attention to the question of the capital invested in the banking business of this country and the volume of the business carried on. In 1890, we had $60,000,000 of paid-up capital; in 1900, $67,000,000, in 1910, $100,000,000 and in 1923, 123,000,000 While during the last 23 years the capital has increased 84 per cent the volume of business done, as indicated by bank clearings and liabilities to the public, has increased 1100 per cent. So that you will see what a disproportion there is in the respective increases. It is true that a large reserve of $123,000,000 has been built up, I will deal with that shortly. In 1900 the bank capital was $67,000,000 and the bank clearings were $1,500,000,000; in 1923 the capital had increased to $123,000,000, and the bank clearings to $17,500,000,000.
But, Mr. Speaker, there is a more significant feature than this. The bank premises in 1890 stood at $4,000,000, in 1900 at $6,500,000, in 1910 at $25,000,000, in 1923 at $70,000,000 plus $6,000,000 in other real estate. Leaving aside the reserves, we find this extraordinary situation, that out of a total of $123,000,000 capital invested in the banking business of this country, no less than $76,000,000 is frozen or locked up in the premises and real estate on which the business of the banks is carried on. In many cases these are handsome pillared institutions of considerable architectural beauty, presenting an appearance of solidity and substance to depositors. Let me repeat that out of a total capital invested in the banking business of

The Address-Mr. Ladner
$123,000,000, no less than $76,000,000 is invested in bank premises. Consequently, leaving aside for the moment the reserves, we have a total net liquid capital of $47,000,000 to carry on the banking business of the Dominion, amounting to $2,686,000,000, which represents the liabilities of all the banks to the public. There arises the extremely important question of confidence in our banking system, which to some extent has been shaken by the Home Bank failure. May I remind hon. members in connection with these figures that in 1890, 1900 and 1910 we had more liquid capital in the banking business than we had in 1923, and I submit that the situation is one requiring the attention of the government.
In order the better to understand my contention, may I ask the House to visualize a base representing $47,000,000 in net capital, and on top of that an inverted pyramid representing $2,686,000,000 liability to the public. The House will thereupon appreciate the delicacy of the situation in the event of business disturbances throughout the world, and it will understand the need for a substantial increase in this capital, or some other arrangement to meet any difficulty which might arise through international complications.
It is not because the business has not been profitable that we find this reduction in the number of banks, because the returns furnished by the banks show that, taking the net earnings or dividends of all the banks, good and bad-and some of them are bad-the dividends paid were: in 1890, 6i per cent; in 1900, 7 per cent; in 1910, 8 per cent; in 1923, 11 per cent, while the reserve has increased from $34,000,000 in 1910 to $123,000,000 in 1923. I suggest that these figures are very significant. But perhaps the most astounding discovery which I made while examining these returns was in connection with the deposits which the public have placed in the banks, and which the banks loan to the institutions of the country to cany on their business. Out of $2,050,000,000 and more of deposits, no less than 70 per cent-and these calculations are practically accurate within i per cent-are to be found in the four largest banking institutions of the country, while the ten smaller institutions endeavour to carry on their business with 30 per cent. The course of events during the past thirty years shows a most interesting development in relation to these deposits and their distribution among our banks. In 1890 thirty per cent of these deposits were in the four largest banks, and
TMr. Ladner.]
seventy per cent in the remaining institutions; in 1900, the percentages were 40 per cent and 50 per cent respectively; in 1910, 45 per cent and 55 per cent respectively; but in 1923, 70 per cent are found in the four largest institutions and only 30 per cent in the others.
Now, in face of these facts, whether in regard to capital, deposits, number of banks, or the creation of reserves, my submission is that unless something is done by co-operation between our banking institutions and the federal government-and the responsibility is primarily on the government-we must ask ourselves-What will be the situation in 1934? For my part, I do not think it is in the national interest or the interest of our banks that the banking business of the country should be centralized in four or five large institutions. When the decennial revision of the Bank Act is taking place we find, and quite properly so, the most experienced and able men in the banking world appearing before the committee to make their submissions. They are the master minds in the banking world. What opportunity has the average member of parliament or the average man in public life of offsetting their advice so far as the public interest is concerned? Though looking after the public interest the member is very seriously handicapped. The point I wish to put frankly before the House is this; the course of events is tending towards a strong centralization of our banking business, and the government, with all its protestations against mergers, combines and trusts, has failed to take any action whatsoever to correct this tendency during last session after an exhaustive inquiry into our banking system.

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would my hon. friend submit his proposals to prevent the tendency he complains of?

maintopic: THE GOVERNOR GENERAL'S SPEECH ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
That is on the next sheet
of my notes, and I shall be pleased to tell him exactly what I would do. I would suggest that as the banking business is a monopoly under our Bank Act, and property so, placed entirely in the hands of our chartered banks, with certain great privileges, such as note issue up to the extent of a bank's unimpaired capital, and likewise with certain obligations -I would suggest that parliament should assume its responsibility to the public and at this juncture stop the course of events by adopting the principles governing the Federal Reserve Bank of the United States and the Bank of England which are applicable to Canada-incorporate them in the Bank Act,

The Address-Mr. Ladner
and give this country an institution which will be representative of both the banks and the people, and so control the course of events which is now only too apparent. We need such an institution. Some of the older members in this House may smile or cast doubt upon my proposal, but if they will study the history of the development of our banking system, and will face the facts squarely and assume their responsibilities to the public, they cannot help but realize the necessity of taking some steps to carry out a proposal on the lines I have suggested. If the government and parliament fail at this juncture to take the necessary action, it is only a question of time when a similar proposal will be put into effect.
These are some of the reasons why we require a reserve bank. We need a check on the rediscount facilities provided by the Bank Act; we should divorce the banking business from the government; we should put it in the hands of the bankers. These rediscount facilities are not complete at present and do not operate to the best advantage of the country. There is hesitancy on the part of the banks to take advantage of them. And we all know the necessity for such facilities.

speechtext: I do not think it is.
